title: The Guardian view on skin cancer: fear the heat of the sun | Editorial
content: With melanoma cases rising, the UK must learn from public health campaigns elsewhere New climate risks bring with them new health risks. An exceptionally warm and dry summer in Europe meant that outdoor workers, and those who choose to spend leisure time in the sun, were confronted more directly than usual by the need to protect their skin from ultraviolet (UV) radiation, as well as avoid dehydration and overheating. In the UK, the annual total of new melanoma cases was reported to have risen above 20,000 for the first time earlier this year (the two most common forms of skin cancer, basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma, are less dangerous). As with other cancers, the increase in cases reflects an ageing and a growing population. A third of those diagnosed with cancer in the UK are over 75. But with the NHS struggling to cope with the number of those seeking treatment, and melanoma the fifth most common cancer – after prostate, breast, lung and bowel (and excluding other skin cancers) – there are growing calls for behaviour change aligned to stronger public health measures. In May, a group of MPs proposed a ban on advertising sunbeds, which – along with sunburn and tanning – are linked with a raised risk of skin cancer. Last year, a group of experts advocated banning their commercial use altogether, as in Australia and Brazil. There are lessons to be learned from other countries besides new laws. In Australia, melanoma is the third most common cancer, and strong public health warnings have been the norm for decades. In 1981, a cartoon seagull was the face of a “slip, slop, slap” campaign aimed at persuading people to slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen and slap on a hat. At school, children are expected to follow a “no hat, no play” rule (meaning no games in sunny outdoor spaces for those with bare heads). While some British nurseries and schools have adopted similar policies, awareness of the risks remains far lower. Many people still habitually welcome bright sunshine and high temperatures. That is partly because these remain much rarer in the UK, especially in northern areas. For good reason, melanoma is less likely to be a priority for health authorities in Scotland than in south-east England. But with global temperatures predicted to keep rising, and given their commitment to shift towards prevention in healthcare, UK ministers and local health bosses should look again at the risks of UV radiation and the factors driving it (the National Cancer Plan has already committed officials in England to seek further evidence on sunbeds). In Australia, doctors have objected to tanning apps promoted by influencers; in the UK there has been an increase in the popularity of tanning among young people, due in part to promotion on social media. Personalised care for many cancers, in the form of immunotherapy, has led to the present being termed a “golden age” for oncology. Such advances deserve to be celebrated. But there are tensions between the desire to focus on innovation and the need to improve access to more established services, and invest in prevention and public health. Melanoma is one of many diseases in which behaviour has a role (cancers linked to obesity are others). After a tightening of the law on tobacco and vapes, and following this summer’s record high temperatures, there is a strong case for renewed efforts to communicate the risks associated with the sun as well as artificial UV light – in time for summer 2027. title: The Guardian view on extreme heat: its scale should be a wake-up call to us all | Editorial
content: With thousands dead across Europe this summer, it’s time to recognise heatwaves as the major natural disasters they are The numbers are now trickling in: nearly 2,900 dead in the UK, at least 35,000 dead across Europe. That’s how many people are believed to have lost their lives in this year’s early-summer heatwaves – the death tolls for the August heatwaves have yet to be counted. In a sense, these people died in a series of natural disasters, similar to the hundreds who died last month after flooding in Nepal, or during the 2024 floods in Valencia, Spain. And yet we do not process these events the same way. Increasingly deadly heatwaves are the most direct and damaging effect of the climate crisis felt in Europe, but they are rarely framed as such. There are some obvious reasons for this. Heatwaves by definition unfold over longer periods than other disasters, they are less dramatic, the majority of those who die are elderly or otherwise vulnerable, and their deaths often take weeks or months to be catalogued and reported, all of which make heatwaves seem less immediate and visible. But while heatwaves will probably never provoke the same visceral shock as earthquakes or tornadoes, it should still be possible to shift the way the public thinks about them, which could save lives and lessen their damage. The first and most obvious change is in the way heatwaves are reported on. The tendency to use images of “fun in the sun” should be balanced by serious examination of disrupted transit and the dangers of living in sweltering buildings. Perhaps the immediate fallout could be made more legible: heatwave deaths might be made more granular with personal detail. Ultimately, governments should report the death tolls and other fallout closer to the actual event – recall that during the Covid-19 pandemic the UK government statistics reporting was tweaked to reflect weekly Covid-specific deaths, which the media and public followed with close interest. More could also be done to make heatwaves feel like a major collective experience, similar to other disasters. Research shows that over time the British public have come to regard heatwaves as a serious problem, one linked to the climate crisis. But at the same time, most people think that they are personally unlikely to suffer any health consequences. Worryingly, work by the British Red Cross showed that a majority of those aged over 75 did not consider themselves vulnerable to extreme heat. It would help to better communicate the risks and potential adaptation measures to vulnerable people, but equally good would be fostering a sense of community responsibility. Currently, the UK government has an excellent system to warn specific sectors – such as medical and care services – about extreme heat. This messaging should be expanded, and voluntary and local groups should be further encouraged to help people at risk. Again the pandemic gives a model here – the Scottish and Welsh governments in particular fostered a sense that we were all in this together. At a society-wide level, a pilot project in Seville, Spain, to name specific heatwaves and give them a categorisation system like hurricanes made early warnings more effective, and also provided an important anchor for news coverage. This simple intervention should be considered in the UK. Changing the way we talk about extreme heat seems a minor thing. But if the public can be helped to recognise heatwaves as the major disasters that they are, lives would be saved and people would be convinced that the difficult work of adapting to the climate crisis is urgent and necessary.
centralIdea: Heatwaves must be recognized and reported as major, deadly natural disasters rather than temporary weather inconveniences to shift public perception, foster community responsibility, and drive urgent climate adaptation.

title: The Guardian view on Burnham’s devolution plans: power must be accompanied by scrutiny | Editorial
content: Vital accountability mechanisms have withered as English devolution has evolved. The government should take note Andy Burnham has criticised Britain’s “unaccountable state” that is at once too powerful and too distant from everyday life. He has made English devolution the central idea of his premiership, but his plan to give England’s mayors unprecedented power and money will have to confront a number of tricky realities, not least a landscape in which scrutiny of local government is vastly diminished. As England’s devolution map has evolved, vital accountability mechanisms have withered. The abolition of the Audit Commission in 2015 deprived Whitehall of information about local government spending. The decision, taken by the then Tory prime minister David Cameron during his “bonfire of the quangos”, coincided with a period when cash-strapped councils were selling off assets and making risky investments. A succession of bankruptcies and scandals have since exemplified the dangers of governing in darkness, including the questions raised at Teesworks, the development led by Ben Houchen, a Tory mayor, where a “culture of excessive confidentiality” has prevailed, according to a damning 2024 government report. There is wide recognition that greater accountability is needed. But Westminster has tended to create top-down mechanisms where accountability flows upwards and local scrutiny is infantilised. The “trailblazer” deals in 2023, for example, gave the mayors of Greater Manchester and the West Midlands greater flexibility over spending, but made them answerable to quarterly select committees of MPs. Under the current public accounting regime, the Treasury appoints an “accounting officer” to each government department, who answers to parliament for their department’s use of money, including that spent by local authorities. Located in Whitehall, these officers lack knowledge of the places such spending impacts. Mr Burnham is right to try to wrest power back from the Treasury and recognise that those closest to a community best understand its needs. His government’s recent pledge to appoint the chief executives of mayoral strategic authorities as “local accounting officers” is welcome. But its plans to give England’s mayors a share of income tax generated in their area (a power that Lord Houchen has said he will use to fund rebates) will demand deeper forms of accountability. The English devolution bill in 2026 created a new Local Audit Office and introduced new powers for scrutiny committees. Both are improvements. A fine place to end up would be the creation of “local public accounts committees”, an idea suggested in the Starmer government’s white paper in 2024. These could be modelled on Westminster’s public accounts committee, whose reports have exposed flagrant misuses of public money. The prime minister wants to take a “place-based” approach to public service delivery. Such local committees, if properly resourced and empowered, could be integral to scrutinising these initiatives. Yet scrutiny isn’t solely the job of officials. The decline of local media poses another problem. Although new local reporting outlets have flourished in cities like Manchester and Birmingham, an estimated 4.4 million people in Britain live in areas without a dedicated news outlet. A robust solution, once mooted by the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, would be a tax on social media giants to fund local journalism. When mayor, Mr Burnham had a media capable of holding power to account. The same cannot be said for too many places in Britain. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? centralIdea: While devolving power and funding to England's mayors is a positive step toward local governance, it must be accompanied by robust local accountability and scrutiny mechanisms to prevent financial mismanagement, especially given the decline of local media and previous audit bodies.

Proposed reforms, such as appointing local accounting officers and creating local public accounts committees, are welcome steps to ensure deeper accountability for devolved funds.
Effective scrutiny also relies on external actors like local media, which has severely declined, necessitating innovative solutions like taxing social media giants to fund local journalism.

title: The Guardian view on music and drama education: reversing elitism starts at school | Editorial
content: The number of students taking creative subjects at A-level and GCSE is at a record low. The arts must not become the preserve of the most privileged How many of the young people who attended Reading and Leeds festival or a Prom this summer will be picking up a guitar or clarinet when they return to school? New figures suggest not many. The number of students taking A-level music is at a record low: under 5,000, a drop of nearly half from 15 years ago. “We are facing the worst-case scenario prospect of A-level music disappearing from English state schools entirely,” warned Deborah Annetts, the chief executive of the Independent Society of Musicians. Music GCSE entries have also fallen. It has the widest attainment gap for disadvantaged students of any subject. Private violin lessons are beyond the purse strings of most parents. The statistics for drama are similarly bleak. A-level drama entries have almost halved in 10 years, with by far the biggest drop in state schools. Forty per cent of state schools no longer even offer music or drama GCSEs. Leading universities have been forced to close music departments and arts courses. The number of teachers training in creative subjects has also declined sharply over the past 15 years. It is no coincidence that the Ebacc, which prioritised core academic subjects at the expense of the arts, was introduced by the Conservatives in 2010. No wonder the worlds of music, theatre and television have become so privileged. “How did British singers get so posh?” asked a recent piece in the New Statesman. Exceptions such as Adele, Raye and Olivia Dean are all alumni of the Brit school, the only state-funded vocational school for the performing arts in the UK. “Learning an instrument and getting up on stage … is now a luxury not every child can afford,” Ed Sheeran wrote in an open letter last year, asking the government to commit £250m of funding for music education. Its 600 signatories included Elton John, Harry Styles and Stormzy. Alison Balsom, the world-class classical trumpeter, has said that her career would not be possible for a state-school pupil now. Julie Walters and Michael Sheen have spoken out about the challenges facing children from working-class backgrounds hoping to become actors. Sir Keir Starmer was hailed as the most musically accomplished prime minister since Ted Heath, playing four instruments as a child and becoming a junior exhibitioner at the Guildhall School of Music. “To everyone who makes music happen – this government is on your side,” the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, has promised. Scrapping the Ebacc last year was a welcome start. Other plans include the National Centre for Arts and Music Education, finally launching this autumn. Andy Burnham, an English graduate and music fan, has already put vocational education on the agenda. Now he must take up the baton for the arts. Mood music is not enough. Every child should have the right to discover their gifts and fulfil their potential. Music and drama help develop discipline, confidence and social skills, and enhance wellbeing. The creative industries – a source of great economic value and soft power on the world stage – must be accessible to all. Reversing elitism in our recording studios, concert halls and theatres starts at school. As Femi Koleoso of the jazz quintet Ezra Collective put it in their acceptance speech at last year’s Brit awards, giving a young person a trumpet or a saxophone might be the solution to many of society’s problems: “Because when you do that, you give them a dream, an aspiration and a goal.” Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Reform’s funding scandal: Nigel Farage has questions to answer | Editorial
content: An undercover investigation raises issues around foreign money, political transparency and the rightwing populist party’s fitness for power Reform UK’s conference was to open showcasing a party ready for government. It did so with two top aides removed after an investigation aired on Channel 4, its finances under police scrutiny and seven in 10 voters, polls suggest, regarding its leader, Nigel Farage, as sleazy – double the number who thought the same of Andy Burnham. Reform, a rightwing populist party, says it will take power back from a corrupt establishment. The latest scandal raises a question: does Reform oppose the influence of big money – or just who benefits from it? Undercover reporters from Verbatim Investigations, founded by journalists from the US Center for Climate Reporting, pretended to be a wealthy American father and his UK-based son who wanted to donate to Reform. In the UK, foreign donations are banned from politics. But that allegedly was ignored. Verbatim’s team filmed their meetings with James Orr, a Cambridge academic specialising in ethics, and Reform’s head of policy, as well as with Dan Jukes, Mr Farage’s close aide. Both have been “removed” from their posts. Reform officials allegedly commissioned £32,500 of polling, arranged for what they believed was a US company to pay the bill, hid the party’s role and used the results to generate favourable newspaper headlines. Verbatim wired the money from a US firm to pollsters JL Partners, whose boss was filmed saying that he should have disclosed that his client was Reform. JL Partners admits procedural “weaknesses”. When the supposed American benefactor later explained the arrangement to Mr Farage over lunch, the Reform leader’s filmed response was not alarm but celebration: “It worked. Boom.” The second main allegation is that the American father was willing to provide Reform with £500,000 through a “permissible” British intermediary – his son. This, if true, would be unlawful. At the lunch Mr Farage does not say that the father cannot be the cash’s source or that the son can legally only donate his own money. Rather, he is filmed saying “thank you both” when it was explained. Gavin Millar KC, a noted media lawyer, told reporters that “there is enough being said, in the presence of Mr Farage and to Mr Farage, for it to be a red flag – for it to be understood as the reality that this money is coming from an American in a disguised form. And he should be questioning that … On the contrary, he seems to be quite happy to receive the money.” In response, Reform says that it has “broken no laws”. Mr Farage told LBC that while his party had done “nothing wrong”, the footage looked bad and hence party aides were suspended. Reform has not offered much of an explanation, preferring to claim that it has “been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded climate change activists”. Political opponents have reported Reform to the police and the Electoral Commission. Reform’s problem is not that two aides forgot about the rules. It is that senior figures appear to have understood them, discussed how to circumvent them and assumed that nobody able to stop them would find out. A party accused of plotting how to get around the law is now promising to impose a “national emergency” so that judges and officials will not get in its way. That is a telling and ominous reveal about how Reform understands power. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on press freedom: to defend democracy, stand up for journalists | Editorial
content: The lack of justice for Daphne Caruana Galizia in Malta casts a shadow on reporters everywhere The acquittal of Yorgen Fenech, who was on trial in Malta for involvement in the murder of the journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, is a devastating blow for justice and press freedom. Nine years after her car was blown up, it seems increasingly unlikely that anyone will be held to account for ordering and paying for her death. Mr Fenech’s admissions that he knew about the murder before it happened, and gave money to the middle-man who paid the killers, make it hard to understand why he was found not guilty on the lesser charge of association. All killings of journalists are wrong. The bomb placed in Caruana Galizia’s car was especially shocking, as such brazen violence is usually associated with war zones or states overrun by organised crime. The fact that this acquittal came two months after those of three men accused of murdering another journalist, Lyra McKee, in Northern Ireland, adds to a grim impression of impunity for killers. While McKee is not thought to have been targeted in the way that Caruana Galizia was, the inability of police and prosecutors to secure convictions in either case points to wider problems. Joseph Muscat resigned as Malta’s prime minister in 2019. But his party, Labour, remains in power, raising questions as to whether the corrupt networks alleged to have been behind the plot have been broken up. The EU and countries including the UK – which has close ties with Malta – must apply pressure. This is all the more urgent given the global context of intensifying attacks on the press, including in Donald Trump’s US. Reporters Without Borders recently warned that political hostility combined with financial pressures could lead to journalism “being asphyxiated”. Physical safety should be regarded as a bare minimum. As well as addressing threats of violence, politicians and others should stand up for press freedom – even when they don’t approve of every outlet or editorial choice. In the UK, a private member’s bill currently seems the most likely route to outlawing strategic lawsuits against public participation (known as Slapps), which are used – by those who can afford them – to block media investigations and silence whistleblowers. But while Labour’s record in office on this issue is weak, recent actions by Reform UK are an anti-democratic disgrace. Nigel Farage’s party kicked off party conference season by refusing to give the Guardian’s city editor, Anna Isaac, and two other journalists passes. While it refused to give an explanation for barring Ms Isaac, the obvious one is that the party wants to punish her. Ms Isaac broke the story that Mr Farage accepted an undeclared £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, a cryptocurrency billionaire. She also found out that donations to Reform UK caused bankers to report potential money-laundering concerns to the National Crime Agency. There is a clear public interest in news about the way that political parties are funded. But as in Nottinghamshire, where Reform UK banned its councillors from speaking to the Nottingham Post, the party has shown its oft-trumpeted commitment to free speech to be a sham. Singling out journalists for bans is not the same as threatening them. But it is part of a populist strategy that combines hollow rhetoric about liberty with an authoritarian approach to people and institutions that place obstacles on the path to power. Pluralism must be defended at home and abroad – and this includes journalists. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Nigeria’s kidnappings: a country can’t prosper when going to school is a danger | Editorial
content: Abductions are resurging and may be spreading to new areas – with young children among the victims. A military response alone won’t work Early last month, Nigeria’s government announced the largest single-day hostage rescue in its history, with the freeing of 300 people who had been taken in raids in two north central states. Celebrations were short-lived. Barely a fortnight later, gunmen abducted up to 600 worshippers from a mosque in Niger state. Nigerians paid kidnappers nearly $6m in ransoms in the year to June, according to a new report from the Lagos-based consultancy SBM Intelligence – more than triple the total in the previous 12-month period. More than 7,800 people were abducted, a two-thirds increase, and more than 1,100 killed, including almost 900 civilians. When Boko Haram abducted almost 300 schoolgirls from their school in Chibok, Borno state in 2014, it made headlines worldwide. Yet around 45 children, mostly aged between two and five, remain missing after they were snatched from schools in Mussa, in north-eastern Borno state, in May. There is growing concern that kidnappings may be spreading to new areas. Forty-six students and staff were abducted from three schools in the south-western state of Oyo in the same month; they were rescued in July. The kidnappings are just one facet of Nigeria’s multiple and overlapping security crises, which may be key to January’s presidential election. Boko Haram, its Islamic State West Africa Province offshoot and other jihadist groups are battling each other as well as terrorising civilians. In the middle belt and parts of the south-west, violence pits predominantly Muslim Fulani herders against largely Christian farming communities. Climate stress and environmental despoliation are intensifying competition over land and resources. Because the two sides fall largely along religious lines, Donald Trump and American evangelicals have presented this conflict as if it were Nigeria’s entire security crisis, rather than one part of it. The repercussions of abductions can be devastating even if hostages come home. Around 100 Chibok girls remain missing, while some returnees face rejection. Kidnapping also drives displacement, economic disruption and school closures, especially affecting girls in a country with a median age of just 18 and pervasive mass youth unemployment. Many schools in Africa’s most populous country have simply closed. A safe schools protection initiative was laudable, but has limited effect without broader security improvements. Successive governments have failed to curb the violence. An overly centralised state and an overstretched security apparatus leave too many of Nigeria’s 240 million people unprotected. State abandonment is forcing communities to seek their own accommodation with the perpetrators. US strikes and a short-lived troop deployment were misconceived, with Mr Trump casting the complex violence, which has killed many Muslims too, as “Christian genocide”. Nigeria needs outside support rather than intervention. President Bola Tinubu announced a major military expansion and pay rise in July. But Christopher Musa, the country’s defence minister, has said that the military can only be 30% of the solution; 70% is socioeconomic. The army’s operational failures and grim human rights record, and the danger of other essentials being cut to pay for boosting defence, also counsel caution. Nigeria’s children and adults can’t be protected without better intelligence, improved collaboration among security institutions and with communities, and, above all, a fairer social and economic deal. title: The Guardian view on Israeli settlements: Britain can no longer look away | Editorial
content: International law, European action and UK public opinion point the same way. Britain should stop helping to sustain Israeli settlements economically In the Commons this week, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, appeared to have accepted the principle of a trade ban between the UK and Israeli settlements, which Britain says are illegal under international law. This is long overdue. The test now is whether his promised “comprehensive reset” deserves the name. Stopping settlement-produced goods at the border is not enough. Britain should prohibit its companies from sustaining settlement activity – by financing, constructing, insuring, advertising – in territory whose occupation it regards as unlawful. The ban must have teeth. The UK can no longer ignore the violence and pressure exerted on Palestinians in the West Bank by Israel’s government, military and settlers. There have been more than 1,400 settler attacks so far this year, according to the UN, against a record 1,800 registered in 2025. An election campaign has only made matters worse. Last month, Israel issued tenders for 1,234 homes in the 3,401-unit E1 development east of Jerusalem. The country’s ministers gave the green light for the controversial settlement – long condemned for effectively bisecting the West Bank – expressly to “erase” the idea of a Palestinian state, the creation of which the UK officially supports. Israeli ministers have reacted with fury, threatening retaliation if Britain imposes sanctions over settlement expansion. This is disappointing, but hardly surprising. Benjamin Netanyahu has accused countries imposing sanctions of “moral bankruptcy”. Yet Britain would be following several comparable European states that increasingly regard such bans as a consequence of international law. Spain has banned settlement imports; Norway is legislating against trade and services linked to settlements; nine EU governments have demanded action from Brussels. Since 1967, Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jewish people among 3.3 million Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem. There are now calls to suspend the EU’s trade agreement with Israel. Britain has such a deal and, under Sir Keir Starmer, Labour wanted to “distinguish and protect trade with people and businesses across the state of Israel”. This gave critics reason to warn that targeting settlements could end up as a “de facto” boycott of Israel. But that gets the argument backwards: Israel cannot make the settlements part of its economy and then argue that other nations must treat them as part of the country. Mr Miliband has political room to manoeuvre. Polling suggests that even Reform UK and Conservative voters are more likely to support than oppose a settlement trade ban. In parliament there was agreement stretching from the Greens to Labour to Tory MPs that something has to be done. Settlement expansion accelerated after Mr Netanyahu’s far-right coalition took power in 2022 and then again after Hamas’s murderous attack sparked the Gaza war in 2023. The legal case is clear: other nations are acting and the political space is opening up – all while creeping annexation becomes a reality. Israel is extending civilian control over occupied territory as settlements expand. Gaza, where more than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed, has understandably commanded the world’s attention. No one disputes that Israel exists in a violent and unstable neighbourhood, though its actions aggravate, rather than alleviate, that instability. But the West Bank and Jerusalem cannot be ignored. Security cannot justify an ideological land grab. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the global bond shock: Andy Burnham should take note | Editorial
content: Japan’s collision with Donald Trump reveals the dilemma facing Britain: economic independence is becoming more necessary – and more tricky to achieve “In the midst of every crisis lies great opportunity” is an aphorism attributed to Albert Einstein. It seems to be taken to heart by this White House. A global bond sell-off sparked by an inflationary shock emanating from the Gulf sees Donald Trump seeking to restrict plans by Japan – a longtime ally – to reduce dependence on an international system America dominates. Japan, a successful exporter, has long done things its own way. For years Tokyo saw off the bond vigilantes despite running enormous deficits and a huge national debt. It demonstrated how a central bank could fund public spending and keep interest rates low if it wanted to. This economic model was refined by Shinzo Abe, Japan’s longest-serving prime minister. However, this week the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called time on Abenomics as his price for US help in stabilising Japan’s currency. Japan’s Sanae Takaichi, he indicated, should shrink her $2tn spending plans and raise rates. Abenomics did not suddenly become financially impossible. It became inconvenient to the issuer of the world’s reserve currency. Kevin Warsh, Mr Trump’s handpicked chair of the US Federal Reserve, has made it clear that he will raise interest rates in response to inflationary pressures. Others will be expected to follow. In Japan’s case, Washington fears that a yen crisis could become a bond crisis. A disorderly rout could force Japan into ever larger currency interventions – and repeated appeals to Washington to help defend the yen. If such aid proved inadequate, Tokyo could end up defending its currency by dumping US treasury bonds – of which it has more than a trillion dollars worth – and put upward pressure on the very yields Mr Bessent is trying to contain. His demand that Tokyo raise rates and cut spending is not just about Japanese inflation. It is about trying to prevent Tokyo’s adjustment to the Iran shock being exported on to America’s balance sheet. Mr Burnham’s first Commons speech as prime minister suggests an expansive programme to raise living standards and get growth through regional reindustrialisation. This, he says, rests on the “bedrock” of fiscal responsibility. Mr Burnham promises an activist state to deal with four decades of underinvestment and privatisation. But retaining Rachel Reeves’s fiscal framework leaves his investment plans hostage to interest rates, debt costs and feverish “headroom” speculation. Turmoil in global bond markets could derail his industrial strategy before it gets going. Japan’s big bazooka spending programme was meant to do what Mr Burnham now says Britain must do on a smaller scale: use the state to rebuild productive capacity, reduce strategic dependence and build its export competitiveness. Tokyo has the fiscal firepower, a central bank able to dominate the sovereign bond market and trillions invested overseas. The UK government could mimic that and change its fiscal rules, its relationship to the Bank of England and the way investment is accounted for. But Japan is Mr Burnham’s problem writ large. The war in Iran made it urgent to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. But the conflict’s inflationary shock makes that objective harder – though not impossible – to pursue. Mr Trump’s team is using its leverage over the yen to restrain Tokyo’s plan to make Japan resilient to external price spikes. Mr Burnham has been forewarned: the Gulf inflation shock wave bolsters the argument for economic independence while making the means of achieving it more difficult. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham must realize that while geopolitical crises make self-reliance urgent, they simultaneously restrict the fiscal headroom needed to finance it.

title: The Guardian view on loneliness: the decline in friendship leaves gen Z exposed | Editorial
content: Problems with housing, jobs and technology have dented young people’s confidence in the future and each other Hope, Raye told a crowd at Reading festival on Saturday, was the theme of a set inspired by her second album. Having established through a show of hands that most of the audience had just done their GCSEs, and after recounting her own rocky road to stardom, the 28-year-old singer led a series of upbeat chants of “it’s gonna be all right”. For anyone who thinks adolescence ought to be a time of optimism, it was a charming spectacle. But a new report from the Institute for Public Policy Research thinktank paints a much gloomier picture. Building on existing evidence of declining wellbeing, such as Alan Milburn’s report on young people who are not in education or work, the IPPR’s researchers found that 11- to 24-year-olds in England (gen Z and older members of gen Alpha) are increasingly lonely. They have fewer friends than young people in the past and are less contented with those they do have. One in 20 say that they have no friends at all. A series of interviews produced worrying evidence of their lack of confidence about the future. They also spoke about problems with concentration that they associated with social media. When asked what they do in their spare time, the most common answer was “doomscrolling”. But while the authors point to “deference to unaccountable tech oligarchs” as one way in which politicians have let younger generations down, their analysis goes wider. It includes housing costs, a shortage of entry-level jobs, student debt, austerity and the Covid-19 pandemic. They conclude that the social contract with youth is broken and needs fixing. This is a deliberately broad-brush study that focuses on what the 10 million 11- to 24-year-olds in England have in common. But it does not gloss over socioeconomic differences. The steepest falls in life satisfaction over the past decade have been in deprived areas; housing is a far more serious blockage on the route to independence for those without family wealth. Noting that the average deposit has risen to £78,000, the report states that “owning a home before your mid-30s has become close to an inherited trait”. With social housing all but impossible to access for most young adults, too many are either stuck with parents or in privately rented flats. Labour has already taken steps to boost the supply of new homes, but must do more to improve young people’s prospects. It is a national scandal that so many are locked out. Adolescence is a complicated time of life, and there is an echo of Sigmund Freud’s idea of “ordinary unhappiness” in the report’s reference to the “ordinary challenges” of growing up. It is hard to leave school and parents, and decide what to do next. This is one reason why supportive peer relationships are so important, and why research on friendship is worthwhile. But while gen Z and gen Alpha deserve attention, their problems should not be viewed in isolation. The weakening of the social fabric around them can be seen as part of a wider pattern that the IPPR rightly links to neoliberalism’s assault on collectivism. There is no single policy lever that can be pulled to mend the missing threads. But governments and councils are far from helpless. Housing, job-market reforms (including limits on AI in recruitment) and a stronger overall emphasis on generational fairness would all make the world a friendlier place for under-25s. title: The Guardian view on Trump’s immigration crackdown: who will have fewer rights next? | Editorial
content: The president’s deportation machine is creating a class of people inside the US who have fewer protections against the power of the state Is the Trump administration creating a group in the US with fewer protections against executive power owing to their immigration status? Its often openly racist actions suggest so. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) claims to target “the worst of the worst” – undocumented migrants who commit violent crimes. Yet the Guardian reported that over half of those arrested in July had no criminal convictions or pending charges. That month, ICE made record arrests and deportations, apprehending 1,500 people and removing 1,100 daily. When campaigning, Donald Trump falsely claimed that Haitians were “eating the pets”. In office, his administration moved to end temporary protected status (TPS) for Haitians. In June, the supreme court let the protection expire, leaving about 350,000 people at risk of deportation to a country gripped by violence and instability. The court’s decision means more than 1 million TPS holders from 13 nations previously considered too unsafe to return to are now at risk of deportation. Many have lived and worked legally in the US for years. Although Barack Obama deported a record 430,000 people in 2013, his administration focused largely on border-crossers. Mr Trump’s crackdown reaches deep into America, targeting those who call the country home. The Economist reports that Trumpian legal tactics have left 1.7 million more immigrants open to deportation. Mr Trump’s dehumanising rhetoric does political work: it turns groups into threats, making harsh treatment easier to justify. By calling migration an “invasion”, he sought to suspend habeas corpus – the ancient safeguard against arbitrary detention. When that proved too much even for Mr Trump, his administration attacked due process instead. In July 2025, an ICE directive quietly rewrote detention policy, treating many migrants arrested inside the US as if they had just arrived at the border, denying them bond hearings. For many, the only recourse was to go to the federal courts. Judges repeatedly ruled the policy illegal yet thousands languish in detention for months awaiting relief. The White House has sought to deport immigrants for protected political speech. Last week, a federal judge ruled visa cancellations for noncitizen students’ pro-Palestinian advocacy unconstitutional. Mahmoud Khalil, a Columbia graduate and permanent resident whose arrest by ICE in 2025 after Gaza protests made global news, is still fighting a final deportation order – a stark threat to liberty. Mr Trump’s immigration crackdown still fires up his Maga base, but is unpopular with many Americans. In one week in July, three ICE encounters ended in death. ICE’s masked thuggishness is a disgrace. So is the president’s cruelty. The Brookings Institution thinktank estimates that more than 100,000 children, three-quarters of whom are probably US citizens, have been separated from their parents during Mr Trump’s second term. The argument within the US right is moving beyond undocumented migrants and noncitizens. Some Republicans are pushing to restrict the rights of naturalised and dual citizens – including their right to run for office. They may be spooked by the success of the Ugandan-born New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose family has Indian roots. Mr Trump has long spoken about – and treated – people differently according to their race. He is still doing so. The US has been down this road before. Abraham Lincoln understood the danger: once equality admits exceptions, where do they stop? Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on regulating big tech: Meta has got off too lightly | Editorial
content: New child safety measures are welcome, but the wider risks posed by these platforms remain unaddressed “Hook, hold, harvest and hide” was how Megan O’Neill, a lawyer for the US state of California, characterised Meta’s business model in the trial that ended last week with an $18bn settlement, to be shared between the states and territories that brought the case. It was a clever way to describe the company’s approach to users’ attention and data. But the sharpness of her words was not matched by the deal. While the strengthening of child safety features is welcome, the tech giant once again batted off efforts to alter its products. Meta’s decision to settle enabled it to avoid any admission of liability. It put a stop to the awkward questions being asked of witnesses including Adam Mosseri, Instagram’s CEO, and the damaging claims made by whistleblowers such as Arturo Béjar. This former Meta safety engineer told the court that his own daughter had been sent unsolicited photos of male genitals on Instagram. The $18bn that Meta agreed to pay over 10 years, some of which is conditional on other platforms making similar changes, will hardly dent its profits (Meta plans to invest up to $145bn this year). More significant by far are its concessions in relation to child users. Safety features will become “opt-out” instead of “opt-in”, increasing the likelihood of their being switched on. Parents will be able to change the settings on young people’s accounts so that their feeds no longer show personalised, algorithmically driven content. A new two-hour daily limit, blocks on use during the night and on notifications during school hours, backed up by compulsory age verification, improve on the current free-for-all. So does the commitment to disable obviously harmful “social comparison” features such as cosmetic surgery image filters. But the package falls short of the restrictions on social media companies’ access to children that Australia, the UK, Malaysia, Indonesia and the EU have either imposed or are in the process of imposing (UK ministers have indicated that in areas where US rules may be stricter, they plan to follow suit). By accepting the terms that they did, while declining to raise the “digital age of consent” (at which accounts can be marketed to children) from 13, this deal’s negotiators left crucial aspects of Meta’s business, including its algorithms and addictive design features, largely untouched. There are good reasons why children’s mental health is a central focus of online safety campaigning. But the harm caused by big tech’s monetisation of attention goes wider. The addictive, tribalist and narcissistic behaviours that platforms are widely recognised to promote have implications for societies as well as individuals. One of many outstanding cases against Meta is being brought by Abrham Mearag, whose father was murdered in Ethiopia in 2021, after Facebook’s algorithm allegedly promoted posts calling for his killing. A US court blocked another case against the company regarding its role in the Rohingya genocide. Measures designed to protect American children from anxiety, depression, unlawful data gathering and addiction are important. But they will not reduce the risk of social media being linked to murderous violence, or undermining democracy, elsewhere in the world. It is now for other courts, or foreign governments, to take the next steps in holding Meta and its peer companies to account for their role as overseers of the global digital commons. title: The Guardian view on the rise of Germany’s AfD: mainstream parties must deliver a bolder response | Editorial
content: The far right is close to winning a state election for the first time since the second world war. A different economic approach is needed to combat it The early autumn has become a time of foreboding and angst in German politics. In the eastern states that have become strongholds for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party, it has regularly made headline-grabbing advances in September elections. Only the refusal of mainstream politicians to form coalitions with one of Europe’s most extreme movements has kept it out of power. This year, the lights are flashing red. Next weekend, when voters in Saxony-Anhalt cast their ballots, the signs are that the traditional firewall may not be enough. In polling, the AfD is currently scoring above 40% in the state, which could win it enough seats to govern on its own. Compared with the last election in 2021, its support has doubled; backing for the closest challenger, the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), has tumbled by almost 15%. Those are startling and alarming figures. Since the second world war, none of Germany’s 16 Länder have been governed by the far right, and in office the AfD would exercise substantial powers over education, policing and culture. The Saxony-Anhalt party – which was classified as a threat to democracy by the security services – has pledged to fully exploit them. The party’s manifesto proposes policies such as the segregation of refugee children in separate schools (in violation of EU law), a nationalist curriculum that would shift the focus away from the Nazi period, and the championing of the “normal family” over “sexual deviations and non-reproductive lifestyles”. Whatever the outcome next weekend, the AfD’s sustained lead in national polls suggests a reckoning is at hand for mainstream parties. Postwar politics in Germany has, for obvious reasons, been founded on a horror of extreme nationalism and a focus on consensus and compromise. But more than one in four voters currently back a party that has discussed a programme of mass “remigration”, which could include passport-carrying citizens deemed to have a “non-German” background. This stark reality has led to suggestions that the taboo on cooperation with the AfD should be dropped, on the basis that exposing the party to the practical realities of governing would reveal the emptiness of its populist promises. That would be a strategy born of desperation and one carrying great risks, not least for the minorities at the sharp end of the experiment. But there is little doubt that despite attempts to ape the far right’s draconian stance on immigration, the political approach being pursued by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition government is not working. As elsewhere in Europe, support for the far right is most concentrated in the ailing industrial regions that were once a source of pride and identity, as well as prosperity. Yet as the country suffers from the double whammy of Chinese competition and US protectionism, Mr Merz’s focus on tax cuts, welfare reform and raising the retirement age is signally failing to address the crisis afflicting Europe’s largest economy. While campaigning in 2018 to become leader of the CDU, the chancellor pledged to halve the AfD’s vote. Support for it has instead doubled. Mr Merz’s own popularity ratings are at a record low for any chancellor, while his coalition partner, the Social Democratic party, is faring just as badly in the polls. A vote next weekend freighted with ominous symbolism will send yet another message to a failing political class that it needs to rethink its priorities.
centralIdea: The unprecedented rise of the far-right AfD party in Germany poses a severe threat to democratic institutions, signaling that mainstream parties must abandon ineffective economic policies and desperate political strategies in favor of a bolder, more systemic response.

title: The Guardian view on rare earths: it’s common sense to secure essential supply chains | Editorial
content: Outsourcing the industry to China cannot continue, but Europe knows it can no longer count on the US for a solution The alarm sounded 16 years ago. In 2010, China blocked exports of key rare earths to Japan in a row over disputed islands in the East China Sea. The critical minerals are essential to everything from advanced weaponry and iPhones to electric vehicle batteries and wind turbines, so the rest of the world took note. But it didn’t take much action. China still accounts for about 70% of rare-earth mining globally and 90% of separation and processing. Then, last year, Beijing forced Donald Trump to back away from his trade war – not with its retaliatory tariffs, but the curbing of rare-earth exports. A scramble for new supplies began in earnest. The year-long trade truce is due to expire in November. The price of erbium, an element essential to communications infrastructure, has already jumped because of fears that export controls will soon be renewed. The 17 metals known as rare earths are far from rare; their name refers to the low concentrations in which they are found. Extraction and processing are costly, complex and often dirty, while returns are low. That’s why the US – which dominated the industry in the 1980s – and others outsourced production to China. Any plan to diversify supply chains must somehow build in predictable demand and pricing to succeed. Even now, US rare earths are reportedly flowing to Asia because of the lack of domestic demand. While “Big shovel” is becoming the new driver of geopolitics, rare earths are a tiny slice of the critical minerals market – worth less than $6bn globally last year. Efforts to diversify supply chains had already begun. But the US-China standoff accelerated them. Last autumn, the Pentagon became the single largest investor in the US firm MP Minerals. In February, the Trump administration announced that it would spend $12bn to create a critical minerals reserve, focusing initially on rare earths. US officials have reportedly described their plan to create new supply chains as a “Manhattan Project” for rare earths. Others question the strategy behind the splurge of money and projects. China, which imports rare earths for processing and has seen them affected by the war in Myanmar, also wants to diversify its supplies. Washington and Beijing are looking to South Africa, Greenland and, in particular, Brazil, raising grave concern about the ecological impact. Innovation, particularly in finding ways to recycle rare earths or extract them from mining waste or runoff, could help meet demand and reduce environmental damage. But it will not stop the extraction drive. Earlier this year, the US launched a critical minerals coalition with 54 partners, including Australia, the European Commission and the UK. A multilateral approach is essential. But Europe and others know it would be extremely risky to count on Washington solely, given the unreliability of the Trump administration, its wild use of trade weapons and its threats to invade Greenland. Stockpiles of essential rare earths, serious investment and stronger partnerships with likeminded allies will be central to a solution. The 2025 European Critical Raw Materials Act set targets for reducing import dependence by 2030. France is already home to the biggest facility outside China to process all 17 rare earths, and a deal for Brazilian minerals is under discussion. But many fear that European countries are moving too slowly. That must change.
centralIdea: The global reliance on China for critical rare earth elements poses a severe geopolitical risk, necessitating urgent, multilateral efforts by Europe and other nations to secure and diversify their own supply chains rather than relying solely on volatile US strategies.

title: The Guardian view on political donations: Labour should curb the power of big money | Editorial
content: Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham favoured a £500,000 donations cap. In office, he’s backing away. That is a mistake On the campaign trail in Makerfield, Andy Burnham told a democracy activist that he favoured a political donations cap of around £500,000 and wanted it reduced over time. His government is now resisting amendments that would move in precisely that direction. Mr Burnham was right in May. He is wrong now. It is difficult to argue that restricting a single person to giving half a million pounds a year to a political party would damage democracy. Such a cap would only affect the mega-rich. Reducing the cap would force parties to wean themselves off the present regime that allows the rich too much say. There are two contra arguments swilling around Labour. The first is that there should be room for wealthy, progressive donors – whose cash helps rebut claims that Labour is in the pocket of the trade unions. The second is the warning from unions that a cap could undermine their ability to contribute to the Labour party. Neither of these arguments holds much water. Whatever benefit Labour might derive from rich friends is dwarfed by the wider damage caused by parties being bankrolled by a few rich individuals. Mr Burnham has registered £345,000 of donations over the past year, including £164,000 from billionaire Lord Sainsbury. In comparison, Thai-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne gave Reform UK a single £9m donation in August 2025 – a sum which exceeds the £8m in trade union donations that Labour will get this year. The timing makes Labour’s retreat baffling. This newspaper’s revelation of Nigel Farage’s undisclosed £5m gift from Mr Harborne in 2024 has turned big money in politics from an abstract concern into a live issue. Reform’s support has fallen markedly in recent months. Mr Burnham could recover the situation by backing amendments from two Labour MPs. Stella Creasy’s changes, which have cross-party support, start with a £500,000 cap – Mr Burnham’s own figure – before reducing it, while allowing parliament to alter the level. She proposes to exclude trade union political funds, recognising that money aggregated from thousands of members differs fundamentally from a donation controlled by a single billionaire or company. The former represents many individual contributions; the latter concentrated economic power. Unions warn that a cap might restrict their political activity. But Ms Creasy explicitly protects their member-funded campaigning cash. Opponents should explain why that safeguard is inadequate. Anneliese Dodds, a former Labour cabinet minister, asks the right question: if ministers believe the growth of big money in politics is a risk, why retain the Conservatives’ sharply increased election spending limits? A donations cap limits how much concentrated private wealth can enter party politics; lower expenditure limits reduce how much money parties need to raise in the first place. Instead of backing these measures, tabled as amendments to the representation of the people bill at next week’s report stage vote, ministers are pressing ahead with elaborate rules governing where political money comes from and how it reaches parties. Yet this year’s Rycroft review, which ministers are responding to, urged parliament, “if it wishes to restore confidence in the political process and to keep big money out of UK politics”, to consider spending limits. Given the scandals of recent years, it is astonishing that Labour is declining to regulate how much political influence any single wealthy donor can purchase. title: The Guardian view on the loan of the Bayeux tapestry: a manifestation of soft power | Editorial
content: The British Museum’s landmark cultural exchange is a symbol of post-Brexit rapprochement between Britain and France “Harold Rex interfectus est”: King Harold is killed. As every British schoolchild knows, the Bayeux tapestry depicts a turning point in the history of these islands: defeat at the Battle of Hastings in 1066, which would lead to the ascent of William the Conqueror to the English throne. Its return to the UK for the first time in nearly 1,000 years is being hailed as a hugely historic moment in its own right. The loan of the tapestry (technically an embroidery of wool on linen) to the British Museum in exchange for UK treasures from Sutton Hoo is the ultimate manifestation of soft power – a 70-metre symbol of post-Brexit Anglo-French rapprochement in comic-strip form. Ticket sales for the exhibition, which opens on 10 September, were the biggest in a single day in the museum’s history, with online queues of 80,000. Radio 4 is devoting a day of special broadcasts to mark the arrival of the tapestry, including a new drama with verse from the poet laureate Simon Armitage. The museum’s videos explaining this tale of ambition, friendship, betrayal and revenge are fittingly narrated by Traitors presenter Claudia Winkleman. Norman-mania is here. “It probably took more years to deliver this project than all the Brexit talks,” Emmanuel Macron joked in a speech to the British parliament last year. To the list of 623 men, 190 horses, 35 dogs and only three women depicted on the tapestry, one might add a 21st-century British king, a French president, and three British prime ministers who have helped to bring it here – not to mention the millions of pounds it has cost. Two previous attempts – one for Queen Elizabeth’s coronation in 1953 and another in 1966 – failed. It would not have succeeded this time if the tapestry had not needed to be moved for renovations to the Bayeux Museum in Normandy. Many curators and restorers still believed the risks of bringing it to London were too great. The late David Hockney called the transferral “madness”. One of his final works, the 90-metre iPad frieze A Year in Normandie, on display this summer at the Serpentine gallery in London, was testament to his lifelong fascination with the tapestry. An online petition against the move attracted nearly 80,000 signatures. However, political will won. From poetry to parody – from Tennyson’s 1876 epic verse drama Harold to an episode of The Simpsons – the tapestry has enjoyed a rich cultural afterlife. But its message has always been political. Napoleon and the Nazis recognised its potential as a propaganda tool. In 2014 Nigel Farage, then leader of Ukip, sported a Bayeux tapestry silk tie during the Rochester byelection, as a reminder of “the last time we were invaded and taken over”. The tie sold out in 24 hours. In these fractured times, the enduring appeal of this 11th-century artefact speaks of a need for a national story. The Bayeux tapestry is a devastatingly human saga. With war raging in Europe, this medieval masterpiece is a reminder of conflict’s brutality, human suffering and the importance of collaboration between countries. The tapestry will return to France for the 1,000th anniversary of William the Conqueror’s birth next year. According to Philippe Bélaval, Mr Macron’s former culture adviser: “Such a loan will only happen once and never again.” This is truly a once-in-a millennium event. Hopefully, its success will pave the way for equally ambitious cultural exchanges in the future. Vive l’entente cordiale! Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on electoral reform: don’t wait for a crisis to fix a broken system | Editorial
content: In an era of multiparty politics, first past the post risks generating perverse outcomes that delegitimise the democratic process If the system that elects MPs to Westminster was obviously the most democratic one available, there would be no need to use alternative modes when electing the UK’s devolved assemblies or England’s regional mayors. The fact that first past the post (FPTP) was not preferred when establishing those institutions reflects an acceptance that there are better ways to turn popular opinion into fair political representation. So why should the Commons stick with an inferior system? This question is raised by an amendment tabled to the representation of the people bill, which returns to parliament next week. The call to establish an independent national commission on electoral reform has been endorsed by 185 MPs. Andy Burnham has backed electoral reform in the past and, as the Guardian reported this week, pressure is growing on the prime minister to translate that view into action: 98 Labour MPs have signed the amendment. For technical reasons related to the scope of the bill, the electoral reform question is unlikely to be put to a vote, but the scale of backbench support compels the prime minister to reaffirm his commitment to change. Downing Street has made it clear that Mr Burnham does indeed back reform but, in deference to the manifesto he inherited from Sir Keir Starmer, accepts that there is no mandate to legislate this side of a general election. That is the constitutionally proper position, but it doesn’t preclude steps that will help win the argument when the time comes. Electoral reformers are haunted by defeat in the 2011 referendum on switching to the alternative vote model – a flawed rival to FPTP that was opposed by the Tories, then the senior party in coalition with the Liberal Democrats. The Labour party in opposition was divided. Back then, the two largest English parties expected their duopolistic hold on Westminster to continue indefinitely. They had few incentives to change a system that suppresses small-party representation. What suited Labour and the Conservatives did not tally with voter preferences, as demonstrated by a steady trend of fragmenting allegiances. Opinion polls show Labour, the Conservatives and Reform UK jostling for support at levels between one-fifth and one-third of national vote share. In devolved and local elections, the Greens, Liberal Democrats and Scottish and Welsh nationalists complicate the picture still further. With multiple parties polling within a few points of each other, FPTP can propel a candidate to victory on a tiny margin and against the wishes of a clear majority of voters. This is a recipe for chaos and disenchantment – conditions that British politics has endured too much in recent years. Delivering stable government is supposed to be a virtue of FPTP. Another is the link between MPs and their constituents, although elements of this can be retained with hybrid systems that also have a proportional element, such as multimember constituencies or combined list and constituency ballots. There is no perfect voting system, but the potential pitfalls of alternatives are not a good enough reason to stick with a status quo that threatens such a perverse outcome as to delegitimise the democratic process. The clamour for reform would then be irresistible. Preparations to modernise the way parliament is elected, and win public support for change, should begin well before that crisis point is reached.
centralIdea: The UK's First Past the Post (FPTP) electoral system is increasingly unsuited for modern multiparty politics, and the government should proactively prepare for electoral reform to prevent a crisis of democratic legitimacy.

title: The Guardian view on child marriage: girls should not be wives | Editorial
content: There’s growing agreement that under-18s need to be protected – but international turmoil is pushing many towards wedlock Every minute, 23 girls around the world wed, according to the Girls Not Brides campaign, a coalition of more than 1,000 organisations across 100 countries. No child should be married. But girls are far more likely to be affected than boys, accounting for nine in 10 of those wed before 18, and their spouses are often much older men. The consequences, beyond the immediate threat of sexual violence, include the shortening of their education, increased risks of poverty and domestic abuse, and poor health, including high rates of maternal mortality. In spring, the Center for Global Development thinktank estimated that child marriage costs $175bn annually in lost productivity and increased health risks. The good news is that the last decade has seen a drop in rates; last year alone, Grenada, Bolivia, Burkina Faso, Kuwait and Portugal introduced bans. But there are disturbing signs of regression elsewhere. In May, the Taliban issued a new judicial code enabling child marriage below the previous minimum age of 16, and preventing wives from ending marriages they entered as children if their husbands object. Previous protections were inadequate and often poorly enforced; now even those have been swept away. Activists say forced and early marriages have soared since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, thanks to the ban on secondary education and the state of the economy. Child marriage is almost double the global average in countries experiencing conflict or other crises, with more than one in three girls marrying before they turn 18, Girls Not Brides reports. The breakdown of economic and support systems, and the exacerbation of factors driving child marriage, such as patriarchal values, can leave families seeing marriage as the only way to protect their daughters – even though they frequently face violence from their husbands. In Gaza, the rate of child marriages dropped from more than 28% in 2009 to just under 18% in 2022. The war has reversed that progress, says the UN Population Fund, with case workers reporting steeply rising rates. Yet child marriage happens in the developing world too. Under-18s could marry in all 50 states of the US until 2018; 17 states have now passed bans, but three – New Mexico, California and Mississippi – still have no age floor. England and Wales raised the minimum age to 18 in 2023; in Northern Ireland, those aged 16 and older can marry with parental consent, and in Scotland they can marry without it. In Australia, 16- and 17-year-olds may marry “in exceptional circumstances”. There is still cause for optimism. Although laws are often evaded – sometimes through corruption, more frequently because marriages are not officially registered – they still send an important message. In Sierra Leone, which raised the minimum marriage age to 18 in 2024, the first trial has begun over the forcible marriage of a 17-year-old. Four men, including the girl’s father and alleged groom, face jail sentences of at least 15 years or fines. The new law allows even guests at the wedding of a child to be imprisoned. Advocacy targeting girls as well as their communities is essential, helping some to resist marriage. Cuts to overseas aid now threaten such work. Child marriage will not end until girls also have educational and economic opportunities, reproductive healthcare and some measure of security. This must be a priority. title: The Guardian view on the French left: division makes Marine Le Pen’s path to the Élysée more straightforward | Editorial
content: Two years ago, progressive parties allied to see off the far right in a parliamentary election. Ahead of a seismic presidential election, that unity is missing In the summer of 2024, as polls suggested that Marine Le Pen’s far-right Rassemblement National party would win a snap legislative election rashly called by Emmanuel Macron, the perennially fragmented French left united to spectacular effect. The New Popular Front, whose name evoked Léon Blum’s anti-fascist alliance in the 1930s, came first in a poll that delivered a hung parliament. Eight months before a presidential contest in which Ms Le Pen is the clear frontrunner, the prospect of a repeat performance appears close to zero. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed, and Olivier Faure, the leader of the Socialist party (PS), have both ruled out the idea of backing a single candidate. Efforts by the Greens to broker talks between progressive parties have fallen on deaf ears. The obvious danger, as the most important election in the history of the Fifth Republic looms, is that chronic division will ease Ms Le Pen’s path to the Élysée. The 75-year-old Mr Mélenchon is a deeply polarising figure who has failed three times to reach the second round of a presidential race. But in a fractured field, the loyalty of his base among the young, the urban precariat and ethnic minority voters gives him a credible chance of making the runoff this time. At which point, polls predict, France’s traditional “Republican front” against the far right would disintegrate, handing Ms Le Pen a crushing victory. Within the PS, the picture is one of confusion and debilitating internal rivalries. Raphael Glucksmann, the leader of Public Square, a small sister movement, declared his candidacy on Sunday and is favourite to win a joint primary. But senior figures such as the former president François Hollande are rumoured to be waiting to make their own move later on. The Greens are divided over whether to offer support to Mr Mélenchon’s uncompromising leftism and reward his new emphasis on the environment, or back Mr Glucksmann’s more centrist strategy. All of which makes Mr Glucksmann’s stated ambition to “rebuild the left” seem somewhat optimistic. A Parisian intellectual married to a famous television newsreader (who has taken leave for the duration of the campaign), he is polling at 10% and is unburdened by the aura of failure that has dogged the Socialist party in recent years. But if he becomes its presidential candidate, he will face the same challenge as his immediate predecessors: how to reconnect with alienated blue-collar towns that now vote for Ms Le Pen, while simultaneously courting Mr Mélenchon’s urban radicals and reassuring middle-class voters who deserted for Mr Macron. In 2022, the former Paris mayor Anne Hidalgo comprehensively flunked that test, receiving 1.75% of votes cast. A historic humiliation was partly the result of progressive voters calculating that Mr Mélenchon was the left candidate with the best chance of coming second, thus excluding Ms Le Pen from the runoff. But as the 2027 campaign begins in earnest, she enjoys a 20-point lead in the polls, and another place in the second round is all but assured. The question, therefore, is who can rally enough support from across the political spectrum to stop her becoming president.
